title: RCMP shooting questions remain, deceased man's dad says
subtitle: RCMP need to take jury recommendations seriously, says Allan Wright
article: The father of a B.C. man who was fatally shot by police in his own bedroom is pleased with the recommendations of a coroner's jury in the case, but says many questions remain unanswered.
Alvin Wright, 22, of Langley was shot in 2010 by RCMP Sgt. Donald Davidson, who told a coroner's inquest that Wright had approached him armed with a hatchet and a knife.

The coroner's jury made seven recommendations, including that police should clearly announce their presence, wear clothing that identifies them in large letters and obtain more information from 911 operators before entering situations.
The jury also said police should have more training in alternate weapons such as Tasers or pepper spray.
Wright's father, Allan, welcomed the recommendations, but said there were still lingering questions about what actually happened.
"The recommendations are helpful if the RCMP take them seriously," Wright said in a news release from the B.C. Civil Liberties Association.

"But at the inquest, we heard that the weapons my son was supposed to be holding had likely been moved; we heard that the bullet casing had been moved; we heard that the closet door that was kicked off had been moved; and the bullet direction through my son's body is completely at odds with the story of the police officer who shot him."
Alvin Wright's widow has launched a civil suit.
The officer who fired the shot was cleared of any wrongdoing by both the Vancouver police and the B.C. Police Complaints Commission.
The police complaints commissioner, Stan Lowe, concluded in his report that the shooting was "reasonable and necessary."
Lowe wrote that Davidson was unable to safely retreat from the bedroom confrontation and feared for his safety when Wright emerged from a closet with a knife.

Lowe's report said the shooting took place only hours after Wright and his common-law spouse Heather Hannon dropped off their infant daughter at the home of Hannon's parents and headed to a bar on Aug. 6, 2010.
While leaving the bar, Wright and Hannon were involved in a heated argument, which continued at their home, wrote Lowe.
Hannon made three 911 calls that night, Lowe's report said, but she later learned from police that Wright couldn't be removed from the residence because his name was on the lease.
Still, Wright and two other officers attended their home, where they confronted Wright.

Lowe said during that confrontation, the officers saw that Wright was holding a hatchet and a hunting knife, and told him to drop the weapons. When Wright stepped towards the officers, Davidson shot Wright, Lowe said.
Toxicology results revealed Wright had a blood alcohol level nearly twice the legal limit for driving.
